en: *Siddhaikavīratantra*, Chapter 2 Edited by Nobuo Otsuka In *Shomonji Kenkyūkai* and *Mikkyō Seiten Kenkyūkai* [Publications]
Taishō University Institute for Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism (eds.), *Studies in the Study of Sanskrit Buddhist Texts* (English title: *The Śrāvakabhūmi Study Group*)
Edited by the Buddhist Tantric Texts Study Group,
Institute for Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism,
Taishō University.
*Studies of the Buddhist Sanskrit Literature*, Tokyo: Sankibo, 1995, pp. 1–9.
One should reveal the King of Tantras to a disciple who is well-awakened, highly enlightened, endowed with virtuous qualities, devoted to the guru, and skillful. (1)
Oṃ, homage to the divine son Vimalacandra! By truth the world is sustained; by truth it is upheld.
By truth the world is established in the Dharma; truth is the eternal Brahman.
Truth is the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, that ocean of virtues.
By this word of truth, enter quickly into the mirror!
Thus:
Oṃ sara sara siri siri suru suru, you who resemble Mount Meru and Mandara, enter, enter! Homage to the son of Kailāsakūṭa!
Tell me truly everything that you have thought to do—
whether for your own sake or for the sake of others, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.

At dawn, having smeared a mandala in a clean place and placed a water jar there, and having performed a grand worship, one should empower a mirror and show it to a boy or a girl who is unblemished, well-bathed, dressed in freshly washed garments, with limbs anointed with white sandalwood paste, and whose neck is adorned with fragrant flowers;
this reveals the intended matter exactly as it is, without error.

In the evening, having smeared a mandala at the location of the head and having performed a great worship of the divine son Vimalacandra, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and sleep in silence; thus,
the intended task will be auspiciously accomplished.
It announces what is auspicious;
for those who recite it constantly, it narrates the events and occurrences of the three worlds. // 20 //
Oṃ, to Śravaṇapiśācinī Muṇḍā, svāhā!
Standing beneath a *vibhītaka* tree or a *vaṭa* tree, one should remain silent and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; then one becomes accomplished (*siddha*).
He will tell the events of the three worlds into one's ear.
Alternatively, having bathed and being clothed in clean garments, one should recite it ten thousand times in a secluded place.
Then success is attained.

At night, having consecrated Kuṣṭha eight hundred times with mantras, one should anoint one's own face and feet and sleep without speaking; in a dream, it reveals what is auspicious or inauspicious. // 21 //
Oṃ, homage to the seven koṭis of perfectly awakened Buddhas!
It is as follows:
Oṃ cale cule cunde, great vidyā, speaker of truth, granter of boons, speak, speak! Svāhā!
According to the previously mentioned procedure, one may speak [to the deity] before a mirror, a conch shell, a lamp, or a vessel of water.
Having washed one's face with water consecrated one hundred and eight times, one who sleeps in silence will see, in a dream, either what is auspicious or inauspicious. // 22 //
Oṃ mucili svāhā / mohani svāhā / dantili svāhā //
This mantra becomes effective when recited ten thousand times.

Having performed a great worship of the Blessed One, the Noble Avalokiteśvara, and having washed one's face with water consecrated one hundred and eight times, one should go to sleep while reciting it with the task in mind.
Without speaking, one beholds the Blessed One in his true form.
And one perceives what is auspicious and inauspicious while asleep. // 23 //
Oṃ, blaze forth! Hūṃ phaṭ!
This heart-mantra of the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, is accomplished by reciting it one million times;
according to the previously mentioned procedure, it reveals auspicious and inauspicious matters in dreams. (24)
Oṃ, homage to the seven Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded.
It is as follows:
Oṃ! In the form of a youth, show, show your own majesty; manifest it, reveal the dream as it truly is! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

Having performed worship according to one's means before a cloth painting or an image of the venerable Mañjuśrī, or before a reliquary containing relics, a recitation of seven hundred [verses] should be performed;
then one will personally obtain a dream and cause it to be seen by others. // 25 //
Oṃ, O Karṇapiśācī, speak into my ear! Hūṃ phaṭ!

Beneath a *piśāca* tree, remaining there in silence and observing the vow of clothing while established in the *trailokyavijaya-samādhi*, one should consecrate a mixture of fish, meat, and *jambūlika* with the mantra, present it as an offering (*bali*), and recite the mantra at the three junctions of the day.
On the first day, a sign will appear;
thereafter, she comes, and one becomes accomplished (*siddha*).
From that time forward, it narrates the events of the three worlds into one's ear;
after twenty-one days, success is achieved even for a slayer of a Brahmin.
Oṃ! Four-armed, six-faced, deformed-faced one! Draw forth Karṇapiśācī! Hūṃ phaṭ!
In a cremation ground, one should recite [the mantra] before the image of Yamāntaka;
within three weeks, Karṇapiśācī is accomplished. // 27 //
Oṃ buddha curu curu mārge svāhā.

At a shrine containing relics, in the presence of the Lord Buddha, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times as a preliminary service (*pūrva-sevā*). Afterwards, having performed worship according to one's means, one should recite it eight hundred times at the time of sleep. Reflecting in the mind, "What was my previous birth, and what will my future birth be?", one should go to sleep.
In a dream, one perceives one's past and future births; of this there is no doubt.
If death is to occur within six months, then one sees oneself or another in a dream without a neck.
Having thus consecrated a mirror, one should look; whoever sees a boy or a girl here as being without a neck will die within six months.

Having made a wick from *srotāñjana* and the root of a white *agastya* tree, one should anoint the eyes with it after it has been consecrated eight hundred times; then one perceives directly all those—whether bipeds or quadrupeds—for whom death will occur within six months, seeing them without their heads. (28)
Oṃ, O you who behold dreams, O you with the eye of accomplishment, tell me my dream, svāhā!
This king of mantras performs all the previously mentioned rites. // 29 //
Oṃ! Aditi, give me Devadatta; cause [him] to be given; svāhā!
The maiden toward whom one recites [the mantra] while standing in the midst of water is given to him alone.
One should perform a recitation of one hundred thousand syllables, or attain great prosperity by performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) of one hundred thousand *priyaṅgu* flowers or *palāśa* flowers.
By performing a fire-oblation at night with fuel-sticks from a milk-tree, one obtains the right to recite [the mantra] directed toward whichever village one desires.
Having performed one hundred thousand offerings of lotuses and bilva fruits, one born of a royal lineage obtains a kingdom;
another attains great prosperity.
Having performed seven hundred thousand offerings of whatever flowers are available, one becomes possessed of inexhaustible wealth. // 30 //
Oṃ, victory! O victorious one! O unconquered one! O undefeated one! Svāhā!
This king of heart-mantras of the four sisters, when recited four hundred thousand times according to the previously described procedure, performs the aforementioned rites. // 31 //
Oṃ, svāhā to Megholkā!
Having performed one hundred thousand oblations with *palāśa* flowers or fuel-sticks, one obtains a hundred thousand pieces of gold;
and one who desires a maiden obtains the maiden of his choice. // 32 //
Oṃ, O you who cause the lotus to bloom, O Lotus, O Mahālakṣmī, grant me sovereignty, O Giver of Boons, svāhā!
This mantra is the heart of Mahālakṣmī; when constantly recited, it bestows supreme prosperity.
By performing a fire-offering with whatever flowers are available, great fortune arises.
One obtains a desired maiden as a wife.
By performing one hundred thousand *homa* offerings of pills of *guggulu* resin the size of cotton seeds, smeared with the three sweets, or by offering lotuses, one attains a kingdom.
*Oṃ nandini varade kiṇi kiṇi khiṇi khiṇi śriyaṃ me dada vauṣaṭ*.
This king of mantras, the heart of Nandinī, performs the rites previously described. // 34 //
Oṃ jambhe mohe svāhā!
Having worshipped the Noble Lady Tārā with karavīra flowers and recited this king of mantras one hundred thousand times, it fulfills one's heart's desire. // 35 //
Oṃ vasudhāriṇi svāhā!
Oṃ śrīvasu svāhā.
Oṃ, svāhā to Vasuśrī!
Oṃ vasumukhi svāhā.
Oṃ, svāhā to the glory of the Earth!

Having meditated on oneself in the form of Jambhala, one should visualize Vasudhārā in the center of a moon disc within one’s own heart—golden in color, two-armed, adorned with all ornaments, and surrounded by four goddesses in the directions beginning with the east—with her right hand in the gesture of granting boons and her left hand holding a cluster of grain. By meditating thus, one fulfills one's desires.

Having made a square mandala out of cow dung measuring two cubits in size, and worshipping it with flowers at the three junctions of the day while performing four thousand recitations, one fulfills one's desires within six months.

By performing four hundred thousand homas with whatever flowers are obtained, great prosperity arises. By reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one attains great fortune. Having prepared one hundred thousand pills of guggulu resin, one fulfills one's heart's desire. // 36 //
Oṃ, O Vasudhāriṇī, give me such-and-such a maiden; cause her to be given! Svāhā!
Abiding by the rules of discipline, having bathed and recited this mantra four hundred thousand times while staying in the midst of water, one obtains the desired maiden.
At night, offering a hundred thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from milk-trees while uttering the name of a village, one obtains that village. // 37 //
Oṃ vasudhāriṇi svāhā!
Oṃ, svāhā to Candrakāntī!
Oṃ, svāhā to Dattā!
Oṃ, svāhā to Vasudattā!
Oṃ, to the Noble One, svāhā!
Oṃ, svāhā to Subhadrā!
Oṃ, svāhā to Guptā!
Oṃ, svāhā to the Goddess!
Oṃ, svāhā to Sarasvatī!

Having drawn Vasudhārā in the center of an eight-petaled lotus on a gold plate, a silver plate, or a copper plate, and having depicted the great yakṣiṇīs such as Candrakānti and the others on the petals in the directions starting from the east—two on each petal—and having enclosed [the drawing] within a casket and placed it inside clarified butter, honey, and sugar, one accomplishes the aforementioned tasks according to the previously described procedure. // 38 //
Oṃ, to Jambhala, Lord of Waters, svāhā!
Oṃ, svāhā to Māṇibhadra!
Oṃ, svāhā to Pūrṇabhadra!
Oṃ, svāhā to the Giver of Wealth!
Oṃ, svāhā to Vaiśravaṇa!
Oṃ, in every direction and intermediate direction, svāhā!
Oṃ keli malme svāhā.
Oṃ, to the one with variegated coils, svāhā!
Oṃ, svāhā to Sukhendrā!
Oṃ, svāhā to Carendra!

Surrounded by eight great yakṣas and accompanied by the Blessed Lady Vasudhārā, Suvarṇavarṇa—holding a *nakulī* and a *bījapūraka*, with a protruding belly and adorned with all ornaments—together with the yakṣiṇīs previously mentioned, grants the sovereignty of the three worlds to those who worship him at the three junctions of the day while meditating and reciting, or who offer eight hundred mouthfuls of water. Furthermore, for one who recites while standing in the midst of water before the crow has cried in the morning, there shall be an inexhaustible abundance of wealth.

Alternatively, having drawn Vasudhārā together with the Yakṣiṇīs in one golden or other precious vessel, and the Blessed Lord Jambhala surrounded by Yakṣas in a second vessel, and having joined them together as a pair, one should wear it;
it bestows the eight great accomplishments— how much more so the other accomplishments?
In the *Siddhaikavīra-mahātantrarāja*, this is the second chapter.
